How to use this guide

Each topic opens with a clear objective, then breaks the work into short, numbered walkthrough steps. Every step is paired with a real screenshot so you can match what you see against your own screen.

Work through it with SharePoint open in another window and try each step as you read. This is a do-it-yourself guide, not something to skim — the settings only stick in your memory once your own hands have been on them.

About the screenshots. The screenshots in this guide are taken from the SharePoint Online Advanced training video produced by Learnit (presented by Faz Karim), used with Learnit's permission. The demonstration site, sample files and sample records shown belong to Learnit, so the names you see on screen will differ from your own — the buttons, panels and menus are identical to what you will find in Afton Chemical's SharePoint.

Topic 1 · Finding Documents Fast

Document Libraries

Source video reference · 00:53 – 19:20
◎

Objective

By the end of this topic you will be able to sort, filter and search a document library to locate files quickly, and build your own custom views — choosing which columns appear, how items are sorted, filtered and grouped, and whether the view is public (everyone sees it) or private (only you). Views are the single biggest time-saver in SharePoint: instead of hunting through a long file list, you save the arrangement once and return to it with one click.

1

Start in the library and read the column headings

Open your team site and click Documents in the left navigation. Before changing anything, get your bearings.

  1. Look along the column headings — typically Name, Modified, Modified By and any extra columns your team has added.
  2. Note the Search this library box at the top. It searches inside this library only, including the text inside documents, not just file names.
  3. The toolbar above the list holds New, Upload, Edit in grid view, Sync and Export to Excel.
💡
Tip: Clicking any column heading gives you an instant sort and a quick filter for that one column. That handles most day-to-day lookups — reach for a custom view when you want the arrangement to stick.
2

Open the view menu

Every library has a view selector at the top right. It is currently showing All Documents, the default.

  1. Click All Documents to drop the menu open.
  2. The top section switches the layout — List, Compact List or Tiles.
  3. Below that sit the saved views for this library, and any views you create will join them here.
  4. The bottom section is where the work happens: Create new view, Save view as, Edit current view and Format current view.
3

Create a view — and decide public or private

This is the most important decision in the whole topic, and it is a single checkbox.

  1. From the view menu choose Create new view.
  2. Give the view a name that says what it does — "Pending approval" or "My documents this month" beats "View 2".
  3. Under Show as, pick List, Calendar or Gallery. List is the familiar rows-and-columns table; Gallery shows large tiles, which suits image-heavy libraries.
  4. Under Visibility, decide on Make this a public view:
    • Ticked — every member of the site sees this view in the menu. Use it for arrangements the whole team benefits from.
    • Unticked — the view is private and only you can see it. Perfect for a personal working filter you do not want to impose on colleagues.
  5. Click Create.
⚠
Watch out: You need edit or design rights on the site to create a public view. If the tickbox is greyed out, you can still make a private view for yourself — ask a site owner if the team needs a shared one.
4

Choose which columns appear, and in what order

Once a view exists, return to the view menu and choose Edit current view. That opens the full settings page, which is where the real control lives. Start with the Columns section.

  1. Tick a column to show it; untick it to hide it. Hiding is not deleting — the data stays, it is just off this view.
  2. Use the Position from Left dropdown beside each column to reorder them, with 1 being the leftmost.
  3. Notice how many columns SharePoint tracks behind the scenes — Created, Created By, File Size, Version, Approval Status and many more are available even though the default view shows only a handful.
💡
Tip: Fewer columns beats more. Show the four or five that answer the question this view exists to answer, and leave the rest hidden.
5

Set the sort order

Scroll down to the Sort section. A sort saved into a view means the list is always in the right order when you open it.

  1. Under First sort by the column, choose the column to order by — Modified, Name, Approval Status, and so on.
  2. Pick ascending (A to Z, oldest first) or descending (Z to A, newest first).
  3. Optionally set a second sort column to break ties within the first.
💡
Tip: Sorting by Modified, descending is the most useful default there is — the file someone touched most recently sits at the top, which is usually the one you want.
6

Understand what a filter actually does

The Filter section is the most powerful part of a view. A filter does not hide files from anyone — it simply narrows what this view displays.

  1. By default, Show all items in this view is selected, so nothing is filtered.
  2. Switch to Show items only when the following is true to start building a condition.
💡
Tip: Filters matter enormously in large libraries. Once a library passes several thousand items, an unfiltered view slows down noticeably, while a filtered one stays fast.
7

Build the filter condition

A condition reads like a sentence: show the item when this column, compared this way, matches this value.

  1. Pick the column under Show the items when column.
  2. Choose the comparison — is equal to, is not equal to, begins with, contains, and so on.
  3. Type the value to match, for example Pending against an Approval Status column.
  4. Add a second condition with And (both must be true) or Or (either will do).
💡
Tip: Two special values make views self-updating. [Me] matches whoever is looking, so one saved view becomes "my documents" for every colleague. [Today] matches the current date, so a "this week" view never needs editing again.
8

Group items into collapsible sections

Grouping turns a flat file list into tidy, collapsible headings — the fastest way to make a long library readable.

  1. Open the Group By section.
  2. Under First group by the column, choose the column to group on — Modified By, Approval Status or Department all work well.
  3. Choose whether groups start collapsed or expanded. Collapsed is better when there are many groups.
  4. You can add a second grouping level to nest groups inside groups.
9

Pick a view style

Further down, the Style section changes how rows are drawn.

  1. Default and Basic Table are the standard row layouts.
  2. Shaded alternates row colours, which makes wide tables much easier to read across.
  3. Document Details and Newsletter give roomier, card-like layouts.
  4. Preview Pane shows details when you hover over an item.
💡
Tip: If colleagues complain they keep reading across the wrong row, switch the view to Shaded. It is a two-second fix.
10

Save, and see the finished view

Click OK at the top or bottom of the settings page to save. The library reloads with everything you configured applied at once.

  1. Grouped items now sit under collapsible headings, with a count of items in each group.
  2. Your chosen columns appear in your chosen order, sorted and filtered as specified.
  3. The view name shows in the top-right selector, and you can switch back to All Documents at any time.
💡
Tip: A view never changes the files themselves — only how they are presented. You cannot break anything by experimenting, so try a private view first and make it public once you are happy with it.

Topic 2 · Tracking Information

Working with Lists

Source video reference · 19:28 – 45:10
◎

Objective

By the end of this topic you will be able to create a Microsoft List, rename and add columns with the right data type, enter records one at a time through a form or in bulk using grid view, and switch the same data into Gallery or Calendar presentations. Think of a list as a shared spreadsheet that validates its own data and never has a "final_v3" copy floating around in someone's inbox.

1

See everything the site holds

Before creating anything, check what already exists — duplicated lists are a common and avoidable mess.

  1. In the left navigation, click Site contents.
  2. The Contents tab lists every library, list and page on the site, with its Type, Items count and Modified date.
  3. Use the Type column to tell a Document library apart from a List at a glance.
💡
Tip: An Items count of 0 next to an old list usually means someone created it and abandoned it. Worth tidying up before you add another.
2

Create the list

From Site contents, click + New and choose List. SharePoint offers four starting points.

  1. Blank list — start from scratch and define your own columns. Most flexible.
  2. From existing list — copy the column structure of a list that already works, without copying its data.
  3. From Excel — upload a spreadsheet and let SharePoint map each Excel column into a list column.
  4. From CSV — the same idea for plain comma-separated files.
  5. Or pick a ready-made Template such as Issue tracker, Employee onboarding, Asset manager or Event itinerary.
💡
Tip: If your team already tracks this in Excel, From Excel is the fastest route and gets everyone off emailed spreadsheets in one move. Tidy the headings first — they become your column names.
3

Rename the default column

Every new blank list arrives with one column called Title. That name tells nobody anything, so rename it first.

  1. Click the Title column heading, then choose Column settings → Rename.
  2. Type something meaningful — Full Name, Asset Tag, Issue.
  3. Click Save.
⚠
Watch out: Renaming changes the display name only; internally the column is still "Title". That matters if you later reference it in Power Automate or a formula, where the original internal name is the one that works.
4

Add a column

Click + Add column to the right of the last heading. A panel opens on the right where you define the new column.

  1. Give the column a Name.
  2. Add a Description — it appears as helper text on the entry form, which quietly prevents a lot of bad data.
  3. Set the Type (covered in the next step).
  4. Optionally set a Default value, and expand More options to require a value or enforce unique values.
💡
Tip: Turning on Require that this column contains information is the simplest data-quality control SharePoint offers. Use it on anything you would chase someone for later.
5

Choose the right column type

This is the decision that separates a list from a spreadsheet. The type controls what can be entered and how it can later be sorted, filtered and grouped.

  1. Single line of text — names, references, short codes.
  2. Multiple lines of text — notes and comments.
  3. Choice — a fixed dropdown. Use this instead of free text wherever you can; it makes grouping and filtering reliable.
  4. Number and Currency — values you need to total or average.
  5. Date and time — gives you a date picker and proper chronological sorting.
  6. Person or Group — links to real Microsoft 365 accounts, complete with photo and presence.
  7. Yes/No — a simple tickbox.
  8. Hyperlink, Image, Location and Managed metadata cover the more specialised cases.
⚠
Watch out: Get the type right at the start. Storing dates as text is the classic mistake — the list will happily accept them and then sort 2 March before 10 February, because it is comparing characters rather than dates.
6

Add a record with the entry form

With the columns defined, click + Add new item. SharePoint builds a form from your columns automatically — no form design required.

  1. Each column becomes a labelled field, using the control that matches its type: a date picker for dates, a dropdown for choices, a people picker for Person columns.
  2. Any column description you wrote appears beneath its field as guidance.
  3. Attach supporting files with Add attachments at the bottom.
  4. Click Save.
💡
Tip: The form is generated live from your columns, so adding a column later automatically adds a field. There is nothing separate to maintain.
7

Enter data in bulk with grid view

Filling a form per record is fine for one entry and painful for twenty. Grid view turns the list into a spreadsheet you can type straight into.

  1. On the toolbar, click Edit in grid view.
  2. Type directly into cells. Move around with Tab and the arrow keys, exactly as in Excel.
  3. Copy and paste works too — including pasting a block of rows straight from Excel.
  4. Click Exit grid view when you are done. Changes save as you go.
💡
Tip: Grid view is the answer whenever someone says a list is "slower than Excel". It usually means nobody showed them this button.
8

Switch how the list is presented

The same records can be displayed several ways. Open the view selector at the top right of the list.

  1. List — the standard rows-and-columns table.
  2. Gallery — each record becomes a card. Ideal when the list contains an Image column, such as a staff directory or asset register.
  3. Calendar — records plotted onto a month grid by one of their date columns.
  4. Use Create new view to save any of these as a named view, exactly as you did for the document library.
💡
Tip: These are alternative views, not copies. One set of records, several presentations — change a record anywhere and every view updates.
9

Build the calendar view

A calendar view needs to know which date column to plot, and what to write on each entry.

  1. Create a new view and choose Calendar as the format.
  2. Set the Start date and End date columns. For single-day items, use the same date column for both.
  3. Choose the column that supplies the title shown on the calendar — usually the name or subject.
  4. Pick the default layout: Month, Work week or Day.
  5. Save, and your records appear on the month grid.
💡
Tip: A calendar view over a list of training sessions, leave dates or deadlines gives the team a shared schedule without anyone maintaining a separate calendar.
⚖
Clearing up the confusion

SharePoint list or Microsoft Lists — what's the difference?

This question comes up in almost every session, and the answer surprises people: there is no real technical difference. The distinction is about the experience you use to get at the data, not about where the data lives or what it can do.

SharePoint list
The engine underneath
=
Microsoft Lists
The modern dashboard built on top of that same engine

When you create a list in the Microsoft Lists app, it is stored as a SharePoint list. Same engine, nicer dashboard.

Side by side

FeatureMicrosoft ListsSharePoint list
Where the data is storedSharePointSharePoint
Underlying technologySharePoint listSharePoint list
Modern interfaceYesYes
Standalone app of its ownYesNo
Reachable from a SharePoint siteYesYes
Ready-made templatesYes — more prominentYes
Mobile app experienceBetterLimited
Power Automate integrationYesYes
Power BI integrationYesYes
Permissions modelSharePoint permissionsSharePoint permissions

What actually happens behind the scenes

Start in the Microsoft Lists app
  1. Microsoft Lists
  2. ↓
  3. SharePoint site
  4. ↓
  5. A SharePoint list is created
Start in a SharePoint site
  1. SharePoint site
  2. ↓
  3. A SharePoint list is created
  4. ↓
  5. It appears in Microsoft Lists

Either route ends in the same place, and the same list is visible from both. You are never choosing between two products — only between two doors into one product.

Which door to use

Reach for Microsoft Lists when…
  • You want to start tracking something quickly
  • You want the friendliest interface
  • A ready-made template will do the job
  • It is a personal or single-team list
Typical uses: issue tracker, employee directory, asset register, training records, task tracker.
Reach for a SharePoint list when…
  • The list belongs to a specific site
  • Several departments will use it
  • You are building a full business process
  • You want it embedded into SharePoint pages
Typical uses: procurement portal, supplier database, audit tracker, risk register, HR portal.

A worked example

Say you need a training attendance tracker. You could open the Microsoft Lists app, create the list, add your participants and start recording attendance — all without touching SharePoint. Later, when you want more from it, you go to the department's SharePoint site, drop that same list onto a page, build a Power BI report from it and set up Power Automate to send reminders. No migration, no rebuild, no export. It was always a SharePoint list.

The practical takeaway: if you are new to SharePoint, start in Microsoft Lists. It is easier to learn and quicker to deploy, and because the list is a SharePoint list underneath, everything you add later — Power Automate flows, embedding in pages, Power BI dashboards, Power Apps forms — just works without moving any data. Learn Microsoft Lists and you have learned SharePoint lists at the same time.

Topic 3 · Controlling Access

Site Permissions & Security

Source video reference · 1:05:58 – 1:12:47
◎

Objective

By the end of this topic you will be able to add members and owners to a site, create your own permission group with a chosen permission level, and — the key skill — break inheritance so that one library or list can be locked down independently of the rest of the site. This is how you keep a single confidential folder private on a site the whole department uses.

1

Open site permissions and add people

Click the settings gear at the top right of the site, then Site permissions. The panel that opens is where most access management happens.

  1. Three standard roles are listed, and the names describe exactly what they can do:
    • Site owners — full control, including changing permissions. Keep this group small.
    • Site members — can edit: add, change and delete content. This is where most colleagues belong.
    • Site visitors — read only. They can open and download but not change anything.
  2. Click Add members to invite people, then choose which group they join.
  3. Site Sharing controls who is allowed to share the site onward with others.
⚠
Watch out: Adding someone as an owner when they only needed to edit is the most common permissions mistake. Owners can change everybody else's access — always ask whether member would do.
2

Go to advanced permissions settings

The simple panel covers everyday needs. For anything finer, click Advanced permissions settings at the bottom of it, which opens the classic permissions page.

  1. Every group with access to the site is listed, alongside its Type and Permission Level.
  2. The standard levels you will see are Full Control, Design, Edit, Contribute and Read.
  3. The Permissions ribbon at the top holds the tools for granting, creating and checking access.
💡
Tip: Check Permissions on this ribbon answers "why can this person see this?" — enter a name and SharePoint reports exactly what access they have and where it comes from. It is the fastest way to settle an access dispute.
3

Create your own permission group

The three default groups do not always fit. You might need, say, a group of external auditors who can read one library and nothing else.

  1. On the permissions page, choose Create Group.
  2. Give the group a Name and a short About me description explaining its purpose.
  3. Set the Group owner — whoever is responsible for its membership.
  4. Under Group Settings, decide who can view and who can edit the membership.
  5. Configure Membership Requests if you want people to be able to ask to join, and whether such requests are auto-accepted.
💡
Tip: Always assign permissions to a group, never to individuals. When someone joins or leaves, you update one group instead of hunting through every library they touched.
4

Give the group a permission level

Creating a group does not grant it anything. Scroll to the bottom of the same page to choose what the group can actually do.

  1. Under Give Group Permission to this Site, tick the permission level you want:
    • Full Control — everything, including permissions. Reserve for site owners.
    • Design — can change the look and structure of the site as well as content.
    • Edit — can add, edit and delete items and lists.
    • Contribute — can add, edit and delete items, but not create or remove lists.
    • Read — view and download only.
  2. Click Create.
💡
Tip: The distinction between Edit and Contribute catches people out. Contribute lets someone work with content but not restructure the site — usually what you actually want.
5

Understand inheritance

By default, every library and list inherits its permissions from the site. Change access at the site and it flows down everywhere. That is convenient, and it is also why one folder cannot be private until you deliberately change it.

  1. Open the library or list you want to secure.
  2. Go to its settings, then Permissions for this document library.
  3. Look for the yellow banner. If it reads "This library inherits permissions from its parent", the library has no access rules of its own — it is simply following the site.
  4. The table below shows the inherited groups and their levels.
💡
Tip: That yellow banner is the single most useful indicator on the page. Read it before changing anything — it tells you whether you are about to edit site-wide access or just this one library.
6

Stop inheriting permissions

To give a library its own rules, you must break the link to the site. This is the deliberate step that makes unique permissions possible.

  1. On the Permissions ribbon, click Stop Inheriting Permissions.
  2. SharePoint asks you to confirm, because this creates a separate set of permissions for this library alone.
  3. Click OK. SharePoint copies the current permissions across as a starting point, so nobody loses access at the moment you break inheritance.
  4. Now remove the groups that should not have access, and add the ones that should.
⚠
Watch out: Once inheritance is broken, this library stops receiving site-level changes. Add someone to Site Members later and they will not get access here — you must add them to this library separately. Break inheritance only where you genuinely need to, and keep a note of where you have done it.
7

Confirm the library is now independent

Check your work by reading the banner again — it should have changed.

  1. The yellow banner now reads "This library has unique permissions".
  2. The group table below now describes access to this library only, and you can grant or remove access here without touching the rest of the site.
  3. To undo it later, use Delete unique permissions on the ribbon, which restores inheritance from the site.
💡
Tip: Before handing the site over, run Check Permissions against one person who should not have access to this library. Confirming a correct "no" is the only way to be sure the lockdown actually worked.
4
Topic 4 · Building the Front Door

Pages & Web Parts

Source video reference · 45:10 – 1:05:58
◎

Objective

By the end of this topic you will be able to build a department page from sections and web parts — adding text, quick links, dividers, document libraries and calendars, arranging them in one, two or three columns, and making sections collapsible so a dense page stays readable. A good page is the difference between a site people bookmark and a site people ask you to email things from instead.

1

Create a page and add your first section

From the site, click + New → Page, give it a name, then click Edit. A page is built from sections stacked top to bottom, and each section holds web parts.

  1. Hover to the left of the page body and click the circled + to add a section.
  2. The panel offers two tabs: Sections for empty layouts, and Templates for pre-built arrangements you can then edit.
  3. Pick a layout to drop it onto the page.
💡
Tip: Sketch the page on paper first — how many rows, and how many columns in each row. Five minutes of planning saves a lot of dragging things around later.
2

Set the section layout, shading and collapsing

Click the section's edit handle to open the Section panel on the right. Everything that controls the shape of that row lives here.

  1. Layout options — One column, Two columns, Three columns, One-third left, One-third right, or a full-width vertical section.
  2. Section background shading — four tones. Alternating shading between sections is the easiest way to make a long page feel organised.
  3. Make this section collapsible — turn it on and the section gets a heading you can click to expand or collapse.
  4. Show divider line between sections for a cleaner visual break.
  5. Default display — whether the section starts Expanded or Collapsed when someone opens the page.
💡
Tip: Give every collapsible section a plain-English name. "Monthly safety reports" tells people whether to open it; "Section 2" does not.
3

Open the web part gallery

Inside any section, click the circled + to open the web part gallery — the menu of everything you can place on a page.

  1. Frequently used sits at the top: Text, Button, Quick links, List, Power BI.
  2. Text, media and content holds Button, Call to action, File and media, Hero and Image.
  3. Scroll for further groups covering documents, sites, news, events and embedded content.
⚠
Watch out: Restraint beats enthusiasm. A page with fifteen web parts loads slowly and tells the reader nothing. Aim for the three or four that answer "why would someone come to this page?"
4

Search for a web part by name

The gallery is long. If you know what you want, type it.

  1. Use the Search box at the top of the gallery.
  2. Type a word such as document and the results narrow to matching parts — Document library, Highlighted content, Quick links, Recent documents, Saved for later.
  3. Hover any result to see a one-line description of what it does.
💡
Tip: Highlighted content is the most under-used web part in SharePoint. It pulls in documents matching rules you set — type, date, keyword — and keeps updating itself, so the page never goes stale.
5

Add and format text

The Text web part is the workhorse of almost every page.

  1. Add it, then type directly into the box.
  2. A formatting toolbar appears above: heading styles, bold, italic, underline, alignment, bulleted and numbered lists, indentation, links and tables.
  3. Use the style dropdown (Normal text, Heading 1, Heading 2…) rather than manually enlarging text.
💡
Tip: Proper heading styles are not just cosmetic — screen readers use them to navigate, and SharePoint search weights them more heavily. Real headings make a page both more accessible and easier to find.
6

Build a Quick links navigation block

Quick links is the single most useful web part for a department page. It turns the page into a signpost for everything your team actually opens.

  1. Add the Quick links web part.
  2. Click + Add links.
  3. Choose a source: Recent, Stock images, OneDrive, Site, Upload, or From a link to paste any web address.
  4. Repeat for each destination your team needs.
💡
Tip: Ask your team which five things they open most, and make those the quick links. That one question turns a decorative page into a useful one.
7

Change how the quick links look

The same links can be presented several ways. Open the web part's edit pane and change the Layout.

  1. Compact — small inline chips, good for many links in little space.
  2. Filmstrip — a horizontal scrolling row.
  3. Grid and Tiles — larger blocks with room for images, which suits a small number of important destinations.
  4. Button and List give plainer, text-led treatments.
💡
Tip: Match layout to count. Under six links, use Tiles or Grid so they feel deliberate. Over a dozen, switch to Compact or List before the page turns into a wall of boxes.
8

Set each link's title, thumbnail and alt text

Click the pencil on an individual link to open its settings.

  1. Link — the destination, with Change to repoint it and an option to open in a new tab.
  2. Title — what the tile actually says. Write it for the reader, not the file name.
  3. Thumbnail — Auto-selected, a Custom image, or an Icon.
  4. Accessibility — alternative text describing the image for anyone using a screen reader.
⚠
Watch out: Do not skip the alternative text. It takes seconds, it is a genuine accessibility requirement, and an image with no description is invisible to colleagues who rely on a screen reader.
9

Surface libraries, lists and calendars on the page

This is where Topics 1 and 2 pay off. You can place a document library or a list directly onto a page — and you can point it at one of the custom views you built earlier.

  1. Add the Document library web part and choose which library to show.
  2. In its settings, pick the view to display — your filtered, grouped custom view rather than All Documents.
  3. Add a List web part the same way, including a list shown as a calendar view.
  4. Place two or three of these side by side in a multi-column section.
💡
Tip: A library web part pointed at a custom view is the most valuable thing on most department pages. People see exactly the documents that matter, already filtered, without navigating anywhere or knowing how views work.
10

Publish, and check the collapsed view

Click Publish to make the page live. Until you do, only you see your draft.

  1. Any collapsible sections appear as clickable headings, honouring the expanded or collapsed default you set.
  2. A reader can open just the section they need instead of scrolling past everything else.
  3. Use Page details to set a thumbnail and description for when the page is shared or appears in search.
  4. Re-publish any time; the page stays live while you edit a new draft.
💡
Tip: Open the published page on your phone before telling anyone about it. SharePoint stacks columns vertically on small screens, and a layout that looks balanced on a monitor sometimes reads oddly on mobile.

✓ Design checklist for a page people actually use

Run through this before you tell the department their page is ready. Every item below works in standard SharePoint with no add-ons.

  1. Start from the Communication site template — it is built for wide, readable, published pages.
  2. Use a full-width section for your banner so it spans edge to edge.
  3. Put quick links in or just under the banner, where the eye lands first.
  4. Use a vertical section for a sidebar of contacts or announcements.
  5. Make the navigation short, clearly worded and consistent — it is still how most people find their way.
  6. Alternate section background shading to separate zones without adding clutter.
  7. Apply your company colours through the site theme rather than colouring things individually.
  8. Add a Hero web part if the page is a landing page for several destinations.
  9. Use collapsible sections for reference material so the page opens short.
  10. Embed a video for anything easier shown than written.
  11. Use the News web part to roll up announcements instead of pasting them in by hand.
  12. Always check the page on a phone before announcing it.
A note on "SharePoint design tips" you may find online. Several popular ideas — tabbed pages, cross-site roll-up web parts, one-click page copying and ready-made design packs — are features of paid third-party add-ons, not standard SharePoint. They are genuinely useful, but they need a licence and an administrator to install. The checklist above deliberately sticks to what you can do in Afton Chemical's SharePoint today.

Quick reference

When you want to…Go toRemember
Find a file fast, one time onlyClick the column heading, or the library search boxSearch looks inside documents, not just file names
Save an arrangement for repeated useView menu → Create new viewTick public to share it, leave it unticked to keep it personal
Make a long library readableEdit current view → Group ByTwo grouping levels; start collapsed when there are many groups
Build a view that stays current by itselfEdit current view → FilterUse [Me] and [Today] as filter values
Move a tracking spreadsheet into SharePointSite contents → New → List → From ExcelTidy the Excel headings first — they become column names
Type in many list records quicklyList toolbar → Edit in grid viewBehaves like Excel, and accepts pasted rows
Show list records on a month gridCreate new view → CalendarSet start and end date columns, plus the title column
Give someone editing access to a siteSettings → Site permissions → Add membersMember, not owner, unless they must manage access
Lock down one library on a shared siteLibrary permissions → Stop Inheriting PermissionsSite-level changes no longer reach it afterwards
Work out why someone can see somethingPermissions ribbon → Check PermissionsReports the access and where it comes from
Decide between Microsoft Lists and a SharePoint listEither — they are the same thing underneathNew to SharePoint? Start in Microsoft Lists
Change a page row's shape or shadingSection edit handle → Section panelAlso where you make a section collapsible
Signpost the five things your team opens dailyPage → Quick links web partUnder six links, use Tiles or Grid
Show a filtered document list on a pageDocument library web part → pick your viewPoint it at a custom view, not All Documents
Keep a long page from overwhelming readersMake sections collapsible, default CollapsedName each section in plain English
